# ISO15693 / NfcV in NFC Magic

NFC Magic reads any ISO15693 tag, and clones, wipes or changes the UID of a gen1 or gen2 ISO15693
magic card. This page is the reference for how that works: the magic types, what each operation
does, what each result screen means, and what it was tested on.

What changed in each release is in the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md).

## Important

- **Every ISO15693 tag shows as a Magic candidate.** Magic status can only be confirmed by writing.
- **A wipe can move a gen1 card's UID**, and the new UID can be all zeros. See [Wipe](#wipe).
- **A wipe can destroy a gen3 card**, and the app cannot tell a gen3 card apart. See [gen3](#gen3).
- **Keep one tag in the field at a time.** See [Limits](#limits).

## ISO15693 in brief

An ISO15693 (NfcV) tag holds three things the app works with:

- **A UID** of 8 bytes, printed starting `E0`. A reader finds tags by their UID, and on an ordinary
  tag it is fixed at the factory. A magic card is one where the UID can be rewritten.
- **Memory**, as numbered blocks of a fixed size, 4 bytes on every card tested. The standard also
  lets a block be locked permanently, after which it refuses writes. (Whether magic cards honour a
  lock was not tested.)
- **System information**, which the tag reports on request: its block count and block size, an IC
  reference naming the chip, and two one-byte settings. The **AFI** says what kind of application
  the tag belongs to, so a reader can ask only tags of one kind to answer. The **DSFID** labels how
  the data is laid out.

A reader talks to tags in two ways:

- **Inventory** asks every tag in the field for its UID. This is how a tag is found, and when more
  than one tag is present their answers can collide.
- **Commands** read or write a block, or set the AFI or DSFID. A command can be **addressed** with
  the target's UID so that only that tag acts on it, or **unaddressed**, which every tag in the
  field receives. ISO15693 reads from several centimetres away, so a tag in a wallet near the reader
  can be in the field.

Commands also carry flags. The relevant one here is **OPTION**: some chips refuse a write without
it, and with it set they answer late, in a way the Flipper's firmware cannot currently receive.

Magic cards change their UID or system information using commands of their own outside the standard
set, or by reusing ordinary block writes at special addresses. Each generation does this
differently.

## The magic types

There are three generations of magic ISO15693 card, differentiated by how each changes its UID. The
app supports gen1 and gen2. gen3 is described here so the risk to those cards is understood.
Proxmark uses `hf 15 csetuid` for gen1, with `--v2` for gen2 and `--v3` for gen3.

### gen1

gen1 cards have no backdoor commands. The UID is written with an ordinary WRITE BLOCK to block
addresses 56 and 57, half in each block, and takes effect at once. An inventory in the same field
session returns the new UID right away. 62/63 are two more registers, which proxmark writes first
and this app calls unlock and commit. What they do is inferred. On all three gen1 chips measured,
56/57 took a write with no unlock or commit sent before it, block 62 refused writes, neither 62 nor
63 has ever accepted one, and none of the four answers a read.

gen1 has no configuration register, so a gen1 card keeps reporting its own block count and IC
reference regardless of what is written to it. Since 56/57/62/63 are registers, a file's data at
those four addresses cannot be stored on gen1.

gen1 card sizes tested were 28, 40, or 56 real data blocks. Every write the app sends to a gen1 card
is addressed.

### gen2

gen2 cards use a backdoor command set. These are used to write the UID and what the card reports
about itself (block count, block size and IC reference), so a gen2 copy reports the same chip as the
original.

All gen2 cards tested had 64 data blocks. When a smaller image file is written to the card, the card
then reports the smaller size, while the blocks above stay readable and writable. A file larger than
the card works the other way: the card then reports more blocks than it holds. For this reason, a
wipe does not trust the reported size, and a clone attempts to read blocks above the file size
before it reports the result (see [Clone](#clone)).

The gen2 backdoor is only reachable unaddressed. On all four gen2 cards tested the backdoor refuses
the addressed form. So another gen2 card in the field takes these frames too, and nothing in the app
can prevent it.

The app attempts to write using the gen2 backdoor first, and then if the UID does not change, falls
back to offering gen1.

### gen3

**gen3 cards are not currently supported by this app.**

gen3 keeps its UID in blocks 16/17, and a configuration signature in blocks 20/21. The card stays
rewritable until proxmark's `hf 15 cfinalize` locks it, irreversibly. The gen2 backdoor does not
change gen3's UID, so any attempt to clone or write the UID stops at the gen1 opt-in. Accepting that
writes 56/57/62/63 as ordinary data: those four blocks of the card are overwritten, the UID does not
move, and the configuration is untouched.

**A wipe can destroy a gen3 card.** The wipe does no magic detection, so it can zero the UID and
configuration blocks along with the rest. Per 0x6r1an0y, who wrote proxmark's ISO15693 V3 magic
support, that **bricks an un-finalized card permanently**; the bricking is their report, not tried
in testing. Tracked in #255.

### Not magic

A tag that is not magic leaves its UID unchanged under the gen2 backdoor, so a clone or a Write UID
stops at the gen1 opt-in having written nothing, and backing out leaves the tag unchanged.

## What each operation does

**Check Magic Tag** shows any tag that activates as ISO15693 as a **Magic candidate**: magic status
on ISO15693 can only be confirmed by writing. ISO15693 tags get their own menu: **Write**, **Wipe**,
**Write UID** and **Info**.

### Info

Info shows the tag's UID, manufacturer and chip type, then what the tag reports about itself (block
count and size, DSFID, AFI and IC reference), then the data in every block. The list scrolls, and
`*` marks a locked block. For NXP chips, Info tells SLI, SLIX and SLIX2 apart, including their -S
and -L variants. If a tag does not report its memory, Info shows "Memory: not reported" and no block
list.

### Clone

**Write** clones a saved `.nfc`: an ISO15693-3 dump, or a SLIX save from the stock NFC app. For
SLIX, it writes the ISO15693-3 data and not SLIX-only settings such as passwords or privacy mode.
Any other file is refused with "This is wrong card".

A clone runs in this order:

1. **The UID** is written first, using the gen2 backdoor. On a gen2 card this also sets the file's
   block count, block size and IC reference. The app then power-cycles the RF field, and reads the
   UID back. Nothing else is written until the card reports the file's UID, so a card that does not
   take it is left untouched. This is why a clone has no confirm screen.
2. **If the UID did not change**, the card is not gen2, and the app stops at **"Not gen2 magic
   card"**. This screen explains what a gen1 attempt writes, what it costs if the tag turns out not
   to be gen1, and whether the file's own data at blocks 56/57/62/63 can be copied. **Try gen1**
   writes those four blocks first, and the rest of the file only if the new UID takes. So a tag that
   is not gen1 loses at most those four blocks, and the failure screen names them so they can be
   restored from a backup.
3. **The AFI and DSFID** are written, and each is read back. If the card does not keep one of them,
   the clone is reported as Partial.
4. **Every data block in the file** is written. The app does not stop at the block count the card
   reports, because only a write shows whether a block really exists. If a block refuses every
   retry, the app reads it, and a block that answers a read is not past the end of the card. A block
   counts as written when the card acknowledges it, or, on a card that needs the OPTION flag, when
   it reads back correctly (see [How writes reach the card](#how-writes-reach-the-card)). On gen1,
   blocks 56/57/62/63 are skipped.
5. **The blocks above the file are read.** A clone only writes the file's blocks, so on a larger
   card everything above them still holds the previous data. A gen2 card also now reports the file's
   smaller size, so an ordinary read would look like a clean copy. The app checks what lies above
   the file and what the card now reports, and notes what it finds.

Block locks in the file are not copied. If a block on the card is locked, its write is refused, and
it is reported like any other refused block.

**A gen1 card that already has the file's UID** passes the gen2 check, because that check only
confirms that the UID matches. This happens when the same file is cloned onto a gen1 card twice.
When the clone then writes blocks 56/57, the UID moves, showing that the card is gen1. The app
switches to a gen1 clone, puts the UID back, and reads it back before reporting. The result is the
same as cloning onto a card known to be gen1 from the start. If putting the UID back does not take,
the result screen shows the UID the card now answers to.

### Wipe

The confirm screen, "Wipe? (gen1/gen2 only)", warns on every wipe that it can brick a gen3 card,
because the app cannot tell which card is on the reader (see [gen3](#gen3)).

The wipe writes zeros to every data block the card physically holds, **including 56/57/62/63**. On a
gen2 card those are ordinary data blocks, and skipping them would leave real data behind. The wipe
does not stop at the block count the card reports. It keeps going until a run of blocks answers
neither a write nor a read, and checks that run a second time before treating it as the end of the
card, so a brief dropout is not mistaken for the end.

A block only counts as cleared if it accepts the zero-write or reads back as zeros. A dead stretch
in the middle of the card, one with a working block above it, is reported rather than ignored.

**A wipe can move a gen1 card's UID.** On gen1, blocks 56/57 hold the UID, so a wipe that reaches
them changes it. After the wipe, the app cycles the RF field and reads the UID again. If it moved,
the result screen shows the UID the card now answers to. That can be all zeros, which is not a valid
ISO15693 UID. How far the wipe reaches depends on both the block count the card reports and where it
stops answering reads, so it only stops short of 56/57 when the card reports a low block count and
also stops answering reads early. A wipe that clears nothing does not re-check the UID, even though
a gen1 card's UID may still have moved. Tracked in #255.

### Write UID

Enter a UID (a valid ISO15693 UID always starts with E0) and confirm. The app writes it using the
gen2 backdoor, and offers the same gen1 opt-in as a clone if the UID does not change. Entering the
UID the card already has is refused.

### How writes reach the card

- **Every write that can be addressed is addressed**: the data blocks, the AFI and DSFID, and the
  gen1 UID writes. So a second tag in the field is not written to. This protects bystanders: a
  reader uses the AFI to choose which tags answer, so changing another tag's AFI could make it stop
  working with the system it belongs to, even though it still reads fine elsewhere. The gen2
  backdoor is the one write that cannot be addressed (see [gen2](#gen2)).
- **Cards that need the OPTION flag get it.** Some chips refuse a write without the OPTION flag and
  return a specific error, which the app recognises. With the flag set, the card answers in a way
  the Flipper's firmware cannot currently receive (see [ISO15693 in brief](#iso15693-in-brief)), so
  the app reads each block back instead of waiting for an answer. TI Tag-it HF-I Plus is one of
  these chips.

### While a write runs

The screen shows progress as "Writing X / N" or "Wiping X / N". **Back is ignored** from the moment
a card is found until the result. It could not stop the write anyway, and stopping a clone between
the UID and the data could leave the card with a new UID and none of the file. Each pass has a time
limit, so the screen is never stuck for the whole block range.

**Hold the card still.** If the card is lifted, every remaining block fails, which looks just like
the card running out of space. So before reporting that a card is too small, the app checks that it
is still there, and a lifted card is reported as removed.

## Reading the result

A clone or Write UID with nothing more to report ends on **"Success!"**. Anything else gets a result
screen. The summary shows the counts and the most important note, and **Details**, where offered,
lists every block and note behind it.

| Screen               | What happened                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Clone finished**   | Everything that fits was written and nothing was lost, but there is a note. It can be: data from before the clone still above the file; a card that answers reads past the block count it reports; a block count or IC reference that differs from the file's, as on gen1; or, on gen1, the four register blocks the file reached with nothing in them. It is also shown when the file is larger than the card but its blocks past the card's end were empty ("Holds X/Y blocks."). |
| **Clone partial**    | Part of the file was not written. The screen gives the most important reason: the time limit ("Timed out at block N", with Retry), a card smaller than the file ("Card too small"), file data at the gen1 register blocks ("gen1: 56/57/62/63 differ"), or an AFI or DSFID the card did not keep ("AFI/DSFID not set").                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Clone failed**     | The UID was written, but no data block was. The card has the UID only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Nothing to clone** | The file has no data blocks. Nothing was written.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Wipe complete**    | Shows "Cleared N blocks. Card claims M." Both numbers are shown without a verdict, because the block count a card reports is a setting. A difference either way is usually harmless: a card cloned from a smaller file reports less than it holds, and a card cloned from a larger one, or one that over-reports from the factory, reports more. Shows "UID not re-checked" if the card did not answer the UID check afterwards.                                                    |
| **Wipe stopped**     | The time limit ended the wipe, with Retry. Details shows where it stopped compared with the block count the card reports.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Wipe partial**     | Some blocks would not clear. Details lists them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Wipe failed**      | No block accepted the zero-write. A wipe cut short by the time limit before anything cleared ends here too, without Retry.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **UID changed**      | The wipe moved the UID, usually on a gen1 card where it reached blocks 56/57. The screen shows the UID the card now answers to. This screen takes priority over a time limit or uncleared blocks, and has no Retry. Details still lists them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Unexpected UID**   | The UID moved, but not to the original or to the one requested. This proves the card is magic. The screen shows the UID it now answers to.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **gen1 failed**      | The gen1 UID did not take, so this is not a gen1 card. Blocks 56/57/62/63 may have been overwritten.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **UID unchanged**    | Write UID was given the UID the card already has. Nothing was written.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Write failed**     | The card was removed before the write finished, with Retry. If it was removed during a gen1 attempt, blocks 56/57/62/63 may have changed. Where offered, Details says the UID was not re-checked.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

Retry after a time limit may get further, but the limit is on time, not on position. If a card stops
at the same block again, it is too slow to finish in one pass, rather than refusing the write.

## Limits

- **Keep one tag in the field at a time.** The gen2 backdoor writes are unaddressed, and so are the
  app's reads and inventories. In particular, the UID checks after a wipe, and after a clone that
  reached blocks 56/57, could get an answer from another tag instead of the card. Addressing cannot
  fix this, because those checks exist to find out whether the UID changed, so they cannot be
  addressed to a UID that may be wrong. A badge holder or wallet near the reader is enough to cause
  this. Tracked as #251.
- **A block that was already dead when the card was placed on the reader** cannot be told apart from
  memory the card never had. The read taken when the card is detected stops at the first block that
  does not answer, so nothing above that point can be checked. If no block above such a stretch
  answers, a wipe treats it as past the end of the card rather than reporting it.
- **Files whose blocks are not 4 bytes.** On the gen2 card tested, the clone set the file's block
  size, and then every data write was refused. The result was "Clone failed", and the card kept
  reporting the new block size until a 4-byte file was cloned back onto it. The gen1 card tested
  refused the writes outright.
- **Cards whose memory repeats** answer a read at all 256 block addresses, so the clone's check
  above the file would mistake a 128-block card for a 256-block one. No gen1 or gen2 card tested
  does this, but two tested tags that the app does not support do.

## Tested on

- **Addressing**, on seven cards with four identified chips: TI Tag-it HF-I Plus (identified by how
  it behaves, not by its UID), NXP ICODE SLIX and SLIX-S, and ST LRi2K, plus two whose chip could
  not be identified. Every one accepts an addressed WRITE BLOCK. On every one, a write sent to a UID
  one byte wrong was checked afterwards against a block holding different data, and had changed
  nothing. So the cards ignore a write meant for another UID, rather than just not replying to it.
- **gen1**, on three chips: ST LRi2K (56 blocks), NXP SLIX (28) and NXP SLIX-S (40). On every one,
  the four-write UID sequence sets the UID, the new UID reads back, and the original UID restores
  exactly. The gen1 wipe risk above was reproduced on the LRi2K, the only card tested where the wipe
  reaches blocks 56/57.
- **gen2**, end to end: exact clones with 28, 56 and 64-block files, a 70-block file reported as
  "Card too small" on a 64-block card, the wipe, and the notes a clone leaves. The backdoor's
  refusal of addressed writes was measured on four cards.
- **gen3**, on one genuine un-finalized card: a clone and a Write UID stop at the gen1 opt-in as
  described above, the configuration signature is untouched, and the card was restored exactly. The
  brick was deliberately not tried.
